title: Come, whoever you are
hook: "come, come, whoever you are" is widely credited to Rumi but likely isn't his
tomorrow: if that quatrain isn't his, which four-line poems are?

segments.voice: Yesterday, a disputed ode, and the habit Rumi's own scholars lived by: check the source. Today, the line Inés wants on the cover.

It's on posters, in yoga studios, on wedding programs: come, come, whoever you are, ours is no caravan of despair. Inés wants it on the cover of her grandmother's program. Here's the odd part. Scholars who've searched Rumi's own books for it haven't found it. It turns up among quatrains credited to an earlier Sufi, Abu Sa'id Abu'l-Khayr, and even that credit is uncertain. And in the Persian, it doesn't quite say come. It says come back.
screen: `ON POSTERS AND PROGRAMS.` → `NOT IN RUMI'S BOOKS.` → `IT SAYS: COME BACK.`

segments.voice: So read the Persian. Baz a, baz a: come back, come back, whatever you are. Unbeliever, fire-worshipper, idol-worshipper, come back. This court of ours is not a court of despair. Even if you've broken your repentance a hundred times, come back. That's not a general welcome sign. It's about tawba, turning back to God. The Quran says it in Pickthall's words: "Despair not of the mercy of Allah, Who forgiveth all sins." And a hadith in Sahih Muslim gives a story to feel it by. A man crosses a waterless desert on his camel, with all his food and drink on its back. The camel wanders off. He searches, gives up, and lies down in the shade of a tree to die. He opens his eyes, and the camel is standing beside him. He grabs the rope and, wild with joy, blurts the wrong words: O God, you are my servant and I am your Lord! The Prophet said God is more glad at a person's turning back than that man was. That's the line's real home: the Sufi world of tawba, where the door stays open after the hundredth broken promise. It belongs to Rumi's world. It just isn't Rumi's poem. Love the line, and give it the right name.
screen: `BAZ A: COME BACK.` · `TAWBA: TURNING BACK TO GOD.` · `THE CAMEL IN THE DESERT.` · `RUMI'S WORLD, NOT RUMI'S POEM.` · then, large: `RIGHT NAME, PLEASE.`

segments.voice: Say it out loud once, the way the Persian means it: come back, come back, whoever you are. Then say its name as honestly as you can: a Persian Sufi quatrain, not Rumi's. Let the rest of the minute hold the line, not the name.
Come: in the Persian, baz a, come back. A call to turn home, even after the hundredth broken promise.
Hold on to this: right name, please, for a line that belongs to the Sufi world of tawba. Four days with Rumi again.

screen: `DAY 1500 COUNTS.` → `RUMI AGAIN · 4 OF 8.` → `TOMORROW: IF THAT QUATRAIN ISN'T HIS, WHICH ONES ARE?`

howItsDone: In Islam, tawba is turning back to God after a wrong, and Quran 39:53 tells sinners not to despair of God's mercy. The 'come back' quatrain is recited in Sufi gatherings and printed widely, often under Rumi's name.

Check the attribution wording: the script says scholars who searched Rumi's books haven't found it, that it turns up among quatrains credited to Abu Sa'id Abu'l-Khayr, and that 'even that credit is uncertain' (Abu Sa'id is not known to have composed most of the quatrains in his name). Confirm against Lewis 2000.

Pickthall 39:53 quoted in part ('Despair not of the mercy of Allah, Who forgiveth all sins.'); check word for word. The popular English 'come, come' version is quoted only in its opening words and 'ours is no caravan of despair' paraphrased; its translator is unclear, so no more of it is quoted.
